items.question: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

children.text: Usually, yes. The City of Columbus requires a permit and plan review for a new deck. The only exception is a deck that is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade, not attached to the house and not serving the required exit door. Decks over 169 square feet also need zoning approval. Suburbs set their own rules.

items.question: Does my deck need a railing?

children.text: In Columbus, a deck more than 30 inches above grade (measured 3 feet out from the edge) needs a 36- inch guard. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.

items.question: Is composite decking hotter than wood?

children.text: Composite gets hot in direct sun, and darker colors run hotter. Trex's heat-mitigating boards, such as Transcend Lineage and certain Select and Enhance colors, stay cooler than its original boards but can still get hot on summer afternoons.

items.question: Can I stain or paint a Trex deck?

children.text: Current Trex decking is designed for cleaning rather than periodic staining. Painting or staining can affect fade-and-stain coverage, and sanding can damage the surface. Identify the product line and follow its specific care instructions; older composite lines have different cleaning limits.

items.question: Can I put a fire pit on a composite deck?

children.text: Not a wood-burning one sitting directly on the boards. Trex notes its decking can soften at temperatures as low as 176°F. Check the product's instructions before placing any heat source on the deck.

items.question: Which warranty covers my deck?

children.text: Manufacturer product coverage and Roof King’s five-year workmanship coverage are separate. Trex residential decking terms vary by line, generally from 25 to 50 years. Your written estimate identifies the selected line and applicable coverage; keep both warranty documents with the project records.

items.question: Do you work on decks outside Columbus?

children.text: Yes, we serve communities across central Ohio. See our
service areas
. Permit rules change at city limits, so your estimate should say which building department applies.

items.question: How do I get a deck estimate?

children.text: Call (614) 490-0123 or book a time online. Estimates are free. Tell us whether you're planning a new deck or have an existing one to repair, resurface or refinish.

cards.title: The View
cards.description: Decide how much you want to see through the railing when you're sitting down.
cards.summary: Which Infill Keeps The View Open?

children.text: Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass give the clearest view at seated eye level. Framed glass and Rod Rail are close behind. Rods and cables read as horizontal lines. Balusters and mesh give more privacy and a more traditional look. Glass panels need regular cleaning to stay clear.

cards.title: Maintenance
cards.description: Each railing material needs different care, and the connections matter as much as the finish.

children.text: Aluminum, steel, composite, glass and cable infill each call for different surface care. Check for loose caps, damaged connectors and post movement after storms or heavy use, and keep the exact railing model on record so replacement parts and cleaning methods match. A painted or stained wood railing also needs refinishing as its coating wears. Our
deck refinishing
page covers wood upkeep. If you keep a wood deck, a Trex railing can still go on it. See tab 4.

cards.title: Budget
cards.description: The railing line, the number of stair runs and the post count drive the cost more than the deck's size does.

children.text: Line and infill: Trex describes Enhance as budget-friendly and Select T-Rail as near vinyl in cost. Signature glass and cable sit at the other end. Linear feet of railing, plus the count of corners, gates and stair sections. Posts and blocking: every guard post needs a solid attachment to the framing. Lighting added to posts and stairs, and any repairs found at the inspection.

cards.title: Code
cards.description: If the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, Columbus requires a guard at least 36 inches high.
cards.summary: The Rules A Railing Has To Meet

children.text: City of Columbus BZS memo CIC #23 quotes Residential Code of Ohio 312.1. It requires "a 36 inch high guardrail" on decks where the grade is more than 30 inches below the deck surface, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The American Wood Council's deck guide adds that openings must not let a 4-inch sphere pass, including under built-in benches. It also recommends measuring guard height from a fixed seat rather than the deck surface. Trex Select comes in 36- and 42- inch heights.

cards.title: Stairs
cards.description: Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail.
cards.summary: Handrail And Step Rules In Columbus

children.text: Handrail 34 to 38 inches high, on at least one side, when there are 4 or more risers (RCO 311.7.7). Risers no more than 8¼ inches. Treads at least 9 inches deep. Open risers must not pass a 4-inch sphere (RCO 311.7.4). The AWC guide calls for a graspable handrail that runs continuously over the full flight.

cards.title: Matching The House

items.title: Lighting, Fasteners, Fascia And Drainage
items.description: These four Trex accessories are planned before the boards go down. Wiring, clips, trim and drainage are much harder to add once the deck is closed in.

children.text: These four Trex accessories are planned before the boards go down. Wiring, clips, trim and drainage are much harder to add once the deck is closed in.

cards.title: Deck And Stair Lighting
cards.description: Decide where light is needed (steps, posts, under the rail) before posts are sleeved.

children.text: Trex says its lights run on 24 volts rather than 120-volt household current, use LEDs, and plug into a standard outlet through a transformer. A photocell timer runs the lights dusk to dawn or for 2, 4 or up to 10 hours, and a remote dimmer is available. Trex lists a 5-year limited warranty on its lights and transformers. Accent lights don't replace the stair light the code expects. The AWC guide (citing IRC R303.7) calls for a light source at the top landing that lights all the stairs, switched from inside the house. Motion or timer switches are acceptable.

cards.title: Hidden Or Face Fastening
cards.description: Grooved boards take hidden clips. Square-edge boards and fascia take screws and plugs.
cards.summary: Why The Board Decides The Fastener

children.text: Trex's Universal Hidden Fastener is self-gapping and comes with a stainless steel screw already installed. Clips only work on boards with grooved edges. Stair treads, picture-frame borders and fascia use color-matched composite screws and plugs instead. The estimate names which fastener goes where.

cards.title: Fascia And Finished Edges
cards.description: Fascia hides the framing at the rim and stairs.

children.text: Trex makes fascia in 1×8 and 1×12 boards, 12 feet long, and says it offers matching fascia for every Trex decking color plus Universal White. It needs no sanding, staining or painting. It's a trim board fastened over the rim, so the rim behind it still has to be sound.

cards.title: Under-Deck Drainage
cards.description: RainEscape makes the space under an elevated deck usable.

children.text: Trex says RainEscape keeps rain, spills and snowmelt from dripping through the boards and lets you create a dry patio or storage area below. It comes in brown or black, and Trex lists a 25-year warranty. It sits below the boards, so routing is settled before the walking surface goes down. On an existing deck, ask whether boards need to come up.

cards.title: Trex DeckLighting
cards.description: Deck lighting helps define steps, railings and the edges of outdoor living areas after dark. Plan fixture locations, wiring access and the power supply before enclosing posts or finishing the underside of the deck.
cards.label: Explore Trex DeckLighting

cards.title: Trex Hideaway Fasteners
cards.description: Hideaway includes fastening choices for grooved decking, face-fastened boards and fascia. Hidden clips attach at the board edges; screws and plugs address other locations. Selecting the fastener by board profile and application avoids using a fascia connection in the walking surface.
cards.label: Explore Trex Hideaway Fasteners

cards.title: Trex Fascia
cards.description: Fascia covers the deck rim and gives stair edges a finished appearance. It is a vertical finishing board, not the structural rim joist or a substitute for walking-surface decking. Dedicated fascia fasteners accommodate movement without treating the board like a deck plank.
cards.label: Explore Trex Fascia

cards.title: Trex RainEscape
cards.description: RainEscape collects water below the deck boards and directs it away through troughs and downspouts. It is most useful when you want to use the space under an elevated deck. Drainage routing and access need to be resolved before the walking surface is installed.
cards.label: Explore Trex RainEscape

cards.title: New Railing On A Wood Deck
cards.description: Trex composite railings mount over wood framing.

children.text: Trex Select post sleeves slide over a 4×4 pressure-treated post. Trex says Select railings go over the deck frame or on the inside of the rim joist. Notched posts and posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist are not allowed. Blocking must be added for extra strength. Aluminum lines use their own post mounts, so we check the framing under each post before ordering.

cards.title: Posts And The Rim
cards.description: Guard posts are only as strong as the joist they bolt to.
cards.summary: What The AWC Guide Calls For

children.text: The American Wood Council's deck guide calls for guard posts of at least 4×4 attached to joists or rim joists of at least 2×8, with hold-down anchors rated for at least 1,800 pounds for a 36-inch guard. It notes that the IRC requires guards to resist a 200-pound load in any direction. Soft or split rim boards are repaired before a new railing goes on. That work is priced on its own line. See
deck repair

cards.title: Ledger And House Connection
cards.description: A railing upgrade is a good time to check how the deck is attached.
cards.summary: What The Ohio Code Requires At The House

children.text: CIC #23 quotes RCO 502.2.2: attached decks must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and the attachment can't rely on toenails or nails subject to withdrawal. It also quotes RCO 703.8, which requires corrosion-resistant flashing where a deck meets a wood-frame wall. If the ledger or flashing is failing, fixing it comes before new railing.

cards.title: Moving Or Adding Stairs
cards.description: A new stair changes the route into the yard and needs its own landing and footing.

children.text: Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to the exit route between the door and the yard, including decks, landings and stairs. Landings and stairs 30 inches or less above grade can be issued a simpler minor permit that needs a final inspection when the work is done. Plan the new stair position around doors, furniture and the path into the yard.

items.question: How high does a deck railing have to be in Columbus?

children.text: At least 36 inches, when the deck surface is more than 30 inches above the ground measured 3 feet out from the edge. That's Residential Code of Ohio 312.1, as quoted in the City of Columbus deck memo (CIC #23). Stair handrails are 34 to 38 inches high when there are four or more risers.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace my deck railing?

children.text: Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to decks, landings and stairs that form the exit route from a door, and a permit with plan review to build a deck. Whether a same-for-same railing swap needs one depends on the work, so call Columbus Building and Zoning Services or ask us to check before work starts.

items.question: Can I put a Trex railing on my wood deck?

children.text: Usually, yes. Trex Select post sleeves fit over 4×4 pressure-treated posts. Trex requires added blocking and doesn't allow notched posts or posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist. We check the posts and rim first, and any repairs are listed separately.

items.question: Which railing gives the best view?

children.text: Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass keep the view most open, with framed glass and Rod Rail close behind. Glass needs cleaning to stay clear. Balusters and mesh give more privacy.

items.question: What's the difference between Trex Signature, Transcend, Select and Enhance?

children.text: Signature is aluminum with baluster, glass, mesh, rod and cable options. Transcend is a substantial composite rail. Select offers composite and metal options, and Enhance is Trex's value line in composite or steel. Trex lists warranties of 50 years for Signature, 35 for Transcend, 25 for most Select and for Enhance composite, and 15 for Enhance steel.

items.question: Can I add lighting to an existing deck?

children.text: Often, yes. Trex says post cap and stair riser lights can be added to an existing deck, while under-rail lights go in with the railing. The lights run on 24 volts through a plug-in transformer, so we plan the wire route and the outlet location.

items.question: Is under-deck drainage worth it?

children.text: It is if you want to use the space below an upper deck as a dry patio or for storage. Trex RainEscape catches water under the boards and carries it to downspouts. It goes in below the boards, so it's easiest during a new deck or a resurfacing.

items.question: Do hidden fasteners work on every board?

children.text: No. Hidden clips need boards with grooved edges. Square-edge boards, stair treads and fascia use color-matched screws and plugs. Your estimate states which fastener is used where.

items.title: Size And Layout
items.description: Size a deck from the activities it has to hold, then check the result against the City's thresholds. A few square feet can change which approvals you need.

children.text: Size a deck from the activities it has to hold, then check the result against the City's thresholds. A few square feet can change which approvals you need.

cards.title: Furniture First, Then The Footprint
cards.description: Lay out the table, chairs or lounge seating you'll actually use, then keep a clear walking route from the door to the stairs.

children.text: Measure the furniture with chairs pulled out, not pushed in. Keep the door swing and the stair top clear of seating. Separate zones, such as dining and lounging, can be divided by a landing or a change in level.

cards.title: Sizes That Change The Paperwork
cards.description: In Columbus, 169 and 200 square feet are the numbers that matter.

children.text: The City requires zoning approval for any deck over 169 square feet, whatever its height or location. The only deck that skips the building permit and plan review is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade at any point, not attached to the house, and not serving the required exit door. Most attached decks need a permit at any size.

cards.title: Height, Guards And The First Step
cards.description: Deck height decides whether you need guards and how many stairs you'll have.

children.text: A 36-inch guard is required where the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The step down from the door threshold to the deck can be no more than 8¼ inches, provided the door doesn't swing out onto the deck.

cards.title: Stairs And Where They Land
cards.description: Stairs are part of the structure, so plan them early.

children.text: Risers can be no more than 8¼ inches and treads at least 9 inches. Open risers can't pass a 4-inch sphere. Four or more risers need a 34- to 38-inch handrail on at least one side. Stair stringers must bear on footings or a post-supported bearing block, not on a patio slab that isn't founded below frost depth.

cards.title: Multiple Levels
cards.description: Two levels are possible, but they're engineered differently.

children.text: prescriptive deck guide (DCA 6) covers single-level decks only. It notes that stairs between levels add loads its span tables don't consider. A multi-level design is planned and drawn for plan review rather than built from a standard table.

items.title: Attached Or Freestanding
items.description: How a deck connects to the house is the biggest structural decision you'll make. It sets the footings, the fasteners, the flashing and sometimes the permit path.

children.text: How a deck connects to the house is the biggest structural decision you'll make. It sets the footings, the fasteners, the flashing and sometimes the permit path.

cards.title: Ledger-Attached Deck
cards.description: A treated ledger board is bolted to the house's band joist and carries one edge of the deck.

children.text: Works when the band joist is solid framing that bears fully on the foundation or wall below. Siding is removed at the ledger so it can be flashed. The attachment must resist vertical and horizontal movement; toenails or nails that can pull out are not allowed. The AWC prescriptive guide describes lateral hold-downs in at least two places within 2 feet of the deck edges, each rated at 1,500 pounds or more.

cards.title: Non-Ledger Deck (Beam At The House)
cards.description: A second beam on its own posts carries the house-side edge, so the wall doesn't carry the deck's weight.

children.text: The AWC prescriptive guide describes this approach where a ledger isn't allowed: brick, stone or masonry veneer, hollow masonry, or a cantilevered floor or bay window. Those posts sit close to the house. Footings within 5 feet of the foundation must bear at the same depth as the house footing. With a basement next to the deck, that means deep footings.

cards.title: Fully Freestanding Deck
cards.description: A deck that doesn't touch the house at all braces itself and must still meet the code.

children.text: The building code says that if a positive connection to the house can't be verified at inspection, the deck must be self-supporting. A freestanding deck in Columbus can avoid the building permit only if it's 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval still applies above 169 square feet.

cards.title: Which One Fits Your House
cards.description: The wall behind the deck usually decides.

children.text: Vinyl, fiber-cement or wood siding over wood framing: a ledger is often possible once the band joist is confirmed. Brick or stone veneer, a bay window or a cantilevered floor: the code doesn't allow a ledger there, so use a non-ledger beam. A deck in the yard, away from the house: freestanding.

items.title: Footings And Framing
items.description: Footings, posts, beams and joists carry the deck. The design follows the local frost-depth requirements, soil conditions and the loads and support spacing for the selected materials.

cards.title: Footings Below the Local Frost Depth
cards.description: Deck footings must reach suitable bearing soil and the locally required frost depth. The approved design identifies their depth and location.

children.text: Footing design also considers the load, soil, nearby foundations and buried utilities. We identify utility locations before excavation and arrange the required footing inspection before the concrete is placed.

cards.title: Footing Size
cards.description: Footing size is set by the area each post supports and the soil.

children.text: the deck area a post carries (its tributary area) and the soil's bearing capacity. Where weak soil is likely, the building official can require a soils investigation. A bigger deck or a longer beam span means bigger footings, not just more of them.

cards.title: Posts And Beams
cards.description: Post size limits how tall the deck can be.

children.text: DCA 6 uses 6x6 posts as the minimum. The Ohio code ties maximum post height to post size and requires posts to be restrained at the footing with connectors or embedment. Beams need full bearing: at least 1½ inches on wood or metal and 3 inches on concrete.

cards.title: Joist Spacing For The Boards You Choose
cards.description: Joist spacing follows the decking, so choose the boards before the framing is drawn.

children.text: Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when boards run diagonally. The Ohio code ties wood-decking joist spacing to board thickness.

cards.title: Lumber For Columbus Conditions
cards.description: Outdoor framing needs lumber and hardware suited to moisture exposure and the proposed deck design.

children.text: Ground-contact members, cut ends, flashing and connector compatibility are considered together. The estimate identifies the lumber treatment and corrosion-resistant hardware, with the applicable code and product instructions guiding the installation.

items.title: Ledger, Flashing And Fasteners
items.description: At an attached deck, the ledger is where the deck meets the house's wall framing. The code is specific about what goes there.

children.text: At an attached deck, the ledger is where the deck meets the house's wall framing. The code is specific about what goes there.

cards.title: What The Ledger Attaches To
cards.description: A ledger is at least a treated 2x8, fastened to the house's band joist, never to siding, veneer or an overhang.

children.text: The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. The band joist behind it must bear fully on the primary structure. DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and cantilevered floors or bay windows. In those cases a non-ledger beam is used instead (Tab 2).

cards.title: Flashing That Sheds Water
cards.description: Siding comes off at the ledger, and corrosion-resistant flashing laps over it so water can't reach the wall framing.

children.text: Columbus's deck bulletin requires approved corrosion-resistive flashing wherever a deck attaches to wood-frame construction. DCA 6 specifies metal flashing of at least 0.019-inch nominal thickness, or an approved non-metallic material. It also says aluminum shouldn't touch lumber treated with copper-based preservatives. The door threshold above the deck is flashed and sealed against splash and melting snow.

cards.title: Lag Screws And Bolts
cards.description: The ledger connection needs specified structural fasteners and spacing for the deck load and the house framing.

children.text: The drawings identify the fastener type, diameter, spacing and connection details. Ordinary nails and unapproved substitutes cannot replace that connection. Opening the house wall may reveal repairs needed before attachment.

cards.title: Hardware Rated For Treated Lumber
cards.description: Treated lumber corrodes ordinary hardware, so every fastener and connector is rated for it.

items.question: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

children.text: Almost always. Inside city limits, a deck needs a building permit and plan review. The one exception is a deck of 200 square feet or less that's no more than 30 inches above grade, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval is also required for any deck over 169 square feet.

items.question: How deep do deck footings have to be in Columbus?

children.text: The approved design must account for local frost depth, soil bearing, deck loads and nearby foundations. Footings are inspected before concrete is placed. A shallow block or an old patio slab is not an automatic substitute for a footing designed for the deck.

items.question: Should my deck be attached to the house or freestanding?

children.text: It depends on the wall behind it. A ledger-attached deck needs solid band- joist framing and careful flashing. If a positive connection can't be verified, the code requires the deck to be self-supporting. Brick or stone veneer, bay windows and cantilevered floors need a beam on its own posts instead of a ledger.

items.question: Can a deck ledger go over brick or stone?

children.text: No. The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. AWC's DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and floor overhangs. A non-ledger deck, with an extra beam and posts at the house, is used instead.

items.question: How far apart are the joists for Trex decking?

children.text: Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when the boards run diagonally. Joist spacing is chosen together with the board line.

items.question: Does composite decking get hot?

children.text: Yes. Trex says all decking can get hot in direct sun, especially darker colors. Its SunComfortable colors reduced heat buildup by up to 35 degrees compared with Trex's original boards in lab testing.

items.question: How tall does a deck railing need to be?

children.text: In Columbus, a 36-inch guard is required where the deck is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.

items.question: Can I finance a new deck?

children.text: Ask our team about current financing for eligible deck projects, then review the lender’s rates, repayment schedule and conditions. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

items.title: Does It Need Refinishing?
items.description: Wood decks give clear signs when the finish has stopped protecting them. Look for water soaking in, graying, and rough or checked boards. You can check the first two yourself in a few minutes.

children.text: Wood decks give clear signs when the finish has stopped protecting them. Look for water soaking in, graying, and rough or checked boards. You can check the first two yourself in a few minutes.

cards.title: The Splash Test
cards.description: Sprinkle a little water on a few boards in full sun and in shade.

children.text: Water beads and runs off: the finish is still repelling water. Water darkens the wood and soaks in: the finish has worn through, and the deck is due for refinishing. The Forest Products Laboratory describes this test for water-repellent finishes, and Cabot uses the same check for stains: if the stain still repels water, it's still working. On a new deck, the same test tells you when the wood is ready to take stain. If the droplets soak in, it can be stained.

cards.title: Gray Or Blotchy Boards
cards.description: Gray is weathered wood, not dirt.
cards.summary: What's Happening USDA Forest Products Laboratory

children.text: research explains that unfinished wood outdoors loses its surface color and picks up mildew, so all species eventually turn gray. It treats graying on a finished deck as a sign the finish needs renewing. Cleaning removes the gray layer before new stain goes on.

cards.title: Rough, Checked Or Splintering Boards
cards.description: Small cracks along the grain and raised fibers mean the surface is drying out and wearing.

children.text: Surface checks are common on deck boards because the sun dries the top of the board faster than the rest. Sanding can take the loose, weathered fibers off before a new finish. A board that is soft, split through, cupped badly or loose at its fasteners needs repair or replacement first. Stain does not fix wood that has lost strength. See
deck repair

cards.title: Peeling Or Flaking Finish
cards.description: Peeling means a film-forming finish is letting go of the wood.

children.text: next coat New stain over a peeling film peels with it. Loose finish has to come off before the deck is refinished, and the estimate says how.

items.title: Stain Types
items.description: Deck stains run from nearly clear to fully opaque. More pigment hides more of the wood. On a surface people walk on, though, more pigment also means more film that can wear and peel.

children.text: Deck stains run from nearly clear to fully opaque. More pigment hides more of the wood. On a surface people walk on, though, more pigment also means more film that can wear and peel.

cards.title: Clear And Toned (Transparent) Finishes
cards.description: Show the most grain and color of the wood.

children.text: Newer or well-kept cedar and decks where you want the natural wood to show Penetrating water-repellent finishes are one of the finish types the Forest Products Laboratory recommends for fully exposed decks. They also wear fastest: FPL notes that a water-repellent preservative used as a natural finish may last only 1 to 2 years. Renewing it is simple: clean, then recoat.

cards.title: Semi-Transparent Stain
cards.description: Adds color while the grain still shows through.

children.text: Most weathered wood decks, including pressure-treated pine Penetrating semi-transparent stains soak into the wood instead of forming a film, so they don't blister or peel. When it's time to recoat, heavy scraping and sanding usually aren't needed. They have to soak in to work. Excess that sits on the surface is wiped off rather than left to form shiny spots.

cards.title: Semi-Solid Stain
cards.description: Masks most of the grain but keeps some texture.
cards.summary: Best For Decks With Mismatched Boards Or

children.text: uneven weathering where you still want some texture to show.

cards.title: Solid-Color Stain
cards.description: Hides the grain completely and looks close to paint.

children.text: Solid-color stains form a film much like paint. The Forest Products Laboratory warns that, unless a product is specially formulated for decks, they shouldn't be used on horizontal surfaces because they lack abrasion resistance and tend to flake. Going back from a solid stain to a semi-transparent one means removing the old film, because a penetrating stain can't soak through it. If a solid look is what you want, we choose a product labeled for deck floors and show you how it will need to be maintained.

The estimate states which method we'll use, and which finish, if any, stays on.

items.title: Weather And Timing
items.description: Stain needs the right temperature and dry wood on both the day it goes on and the night after. In central Ohio, spring and fall afternoons can feel warm enough while the boards are still cold or damp from the night, so we plan around the wood as well as the forecast.

children.text: Stain needs the right temperature and dry wood on both the day it goes on and the night after. In central Ohio, spring and fall afternoons can feel warm enough while the boards are still cold or damp from the night, so we plan around the wood as well as the forecast.

cards.title: Air And Board Temperature
cards.description: Both the air and the wood must be within the selected finish’s application range.

children.text: Cabot gives 50–90°F for its general deck-staining guidance. The coating’s own label controls the job; direct sun can make the boards much hotter than the forecast air temperature.

cards.title: Rain And Dew
cards.description: Fresh stain needs a dry stretch to set.

children.text: Manufacturers call for a rain-free window after application. Cabot asks for a day with no rain expected for 24 hours, and notes that wet or cold weather can double drying time. We check the National Weather Service's hourly forecast for your address, including overnight temperature, dew point and rain chances.

children.text: Hose off debris, then scrub with warm soapy water and a soft-bristle brush. Trex recommends a composite deck cleaner twice a year. Trex says not to pressure wash these lines, because it can damage the surface and void the warranty.

items.question: How do I know if my deck needs refinishing?

children.text: Splash some water on the boards. If it beads up, the finish is still working. If the wood darkens and soaks it up, or the deck has turned gray, it's time to refinish. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory and stain maker Cabot both describe this check.

items.question: Can a new stain go over the old one?

children.text: Sometimes. A sound penetrating stain can often be cleaned and recoated with a compatible product. A peeling finish, or a solid stain you want to swap for a semi-transparent, has to come off first.

items.question: Is a semi-transparent or solid stain better for a deck?

children.text: For most wood decks, a semi-transparent stain lasts better underfoot because it soaks in instead of forming a film that can peel. A solid stain hides more, but use one only if it's made for deck floors.

items.question: What weather do you need to stain a deck in Columbus?

children.text: The boards must be dry, air and surface temperatures must fit the selected coating’s label, and the forecast must provide its required drying window. Cabot’s general deck guidance gives 50–90°F; individual finishes can have different rain, dew and curing requirements.

items.question: How soon can we use the deck after staining?

children.text: Dry-to-touch, foot-traffic and furniture times can differ. We provide the selected coating’s instructions and allow for the actual weather rather than promising one return-to-use time for every finish.

items.question: Can you stain or sand a Trex deck?

children.text: No. Trex composite gets cleaned, not stained, and Trex doesn't recommend sanding. Its care page gives pressure-washing limits for its newer lines and says not to pressure wash the older ones.

items.question: Do I need a permit to refinish my deck in Columbus?

children.text: The City of Columbus lists exterior painting among the projects that don't need a permit, and staining isn't listed separately. Building a deck does need a permit and plan review. Historic or special districts may need other approvals.

items.question: Will refinishing hide replaced boards and old marks?

children.text: Not completely. New boards, weathering and grain differences can still show after staining. A semi-solid or solid stain evens out color more, and we go over the expected look before work begins.

items.title: Framing, Ledger And Flashing
items.description: The joists, beams and ledger carry the deck. The ledger is the board bolted to the house, and NADRA calls it "a common source of deck failure." That's why we check it on every repair visit where it can be reached.

children.text: The joists, beams and ledger carry the deck. The ledger is the board bolted to the house, and NADRA calls it "a common source of deck failure." That's why we check it on every repair visit where it can be reached.

cards.title: Ledger Attachment
cards.description: The connection to the house has to resist both downward and sideways movement.

children.text: Columbus requires and what we look for City of Columbus guidance (Residential Code of Ohio 502.2.2) says an attached deck must resist vertical and horizontal movement and may not rely on toenails or nails subject to withdrawal. NADRA's checklist says the ledger should not be fastened with only nails. We look for missing or rusted bolts, crushed or rotted wood at the ledger, and a gap opening between the deck and the house.

cards.title: Ledger Flashing
cards.description: Flashing keeps water out of the house wall and away from the ledger.

children.text: Columbus guidance (RCO 703.8) requires corrosion-resistant flashing where a deck attaches to a wood-frame wall, so water can't enter the wall cavity or reach the structure. Missing or failed flashing can rot the ledger and the house rim joist behind it. Fixing that may mean removing boards near the house and opening the siding at the deck line. We note in the estimate when the wall behind the ledger can only be judged once it is opened.

items.question: Do I need a permit to repair my deck in Columbus?

children.text: It depends on what the repair changes. City of Columbus guidance requires plan approval and permits for alterations to the exit path from the house, which includes landings, decks and stairs. The only exception is a deck that is 200 sq ft or less, no more than 30 inches above grade, freestanding and not serving the required exit door. Low stairs and landings can be issued a minor permit that needs a final inspection.

items.question: Can you replace just the damaged boards?

children.text: Often, yes, if the joists under them are sound. We check the framing first, and the work area can grow if we need access below. Some color difference between new and weathered boards is normal.

items.question: How do I know if my deck is safe to use?

children.text: Warning signs include soft wood, boards or stairs that sag, a deck that sways, loose railings, rusted connectors, and a gap where the deck meets the house. NADRA recommends a professional evaluation, and if you notice any of these, keep people off that area until it's checked.

items.question: What is a ledger board, and why does it matter?

children.text: It's the board that attaches the deck to your house. NADRA calls it a common source of deck failure. Columbus requires attached decks to resist vertical and horizontal movement without relying on nails that can pull out, plus corrosion-resistant flashing at the wall.

items.question: Can new composite boards go on my existing framing?

children.text: Only when the framing is sound and meets the product's requirements. Trex lists pressure-treated lumber or steel as its recommended substructure, and spacing and condition need checking before resurfacing. See
deck replacement and resurfacing

items.question: A storm or tree limb damaged my deck. What should I do?

children.text: Keep everyone off it, photograph the damage from a safe position, and contact your insurer about its reporting process. Then call us to look at the deck along with any other exterior damage. Our estimate describes the damage and the repair; it doesn't decide a claim.

items.question: Should I stain or seal before or after repairs?

children.text: After. Fix the boards and framing first so a new finish doesn't hide a problem, then plan
deck refinishing
for wood decks. For Trex boards, Trex says painting or staining isn't recommended and may void the fade and stain warranty.

items.title: Signs It's Time To Replace
items.description: A deck needs replacing when the problems reach the parts that hold it up: the ledger, posts, footings, joists and railing connections. Damage limited to a few boards or one loose rail is a repair. For that, see [deck repair](/decks/repairs/). Age catches up with decks everywhere. NADRA, the North American Deck and Railing Association, estimates that about 30 million of the 60 million decks in the U.S. have outlived their useful life.

. Age catches up with decks everywhere. NADRA, the North American Deck and Railing Association, estimates that about 30 million of the 60 million decks in the U.S. have outlived their useful life.

cards.title: Rot In The Frame, Not Just The Boards
cards.description: Soft wood in the joists, beams or rim means the structure under the surface is failing.

children.text: Joist ends and the tops of joists, where water sits under the boards The ledger and the house rim joist behind it Beam ends and post tops, where wood meets wood Posts at grade, especially where soil or mulch is piled against them Decay in one board is a repair. Decay in several joists or at the ledger usually means rebuilding rather than resurfacing. NADRA's consumer checklist names decaying materials as a key warning sign.

cards.title: A Loose Or Poorly Attached Ledger
cards.description: The ledger is the board that ties the deck to your house.

children.text: ledger looks like Columbus's deck bulletin says an attached deck must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and it can't be attached with toenails or nails that can pull out. The American Wood Council's deck guide (DCA 6) calls for ½-inch lag screws or bolts and corrosion-resistant flashing at the wall. It prohibits fastening a ledger to brick veneer, hollow masonry or a cantilevered floor overhang. Warning signs: A gap opening between the ledger and the house A ledger held with nails only Missing or rusted flashing above the ledger Water stains or soft wood on the house framing below it Fixing a ledger properly means taking up the boards along the house, which is often the point where a full replacement makes more sense.

cards.title: Failing Posts And Footings
cards.description: Posts that lean, rot at the base or sit on blocks at ground level can't be fixed from the deck surface.

children.text: What current practice calls for DCA 6 prescribes posts of at least 6x6. The beam must sit on a notched post or a post cap, not be bolted to the side of the post. Footings bear on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches below grade or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Many older decks have 4x4 posts, beams bolted to the side of the posts, or shallow pier blocks. New boards don't change any of that; correcting it means rebuilding the substructure.

cards.title: Soft, Springy Or Split Boards Across The Deck
cards.description: When the whole surface bounces, cups or splits, the cause is often underneath.

children.text: Boards or joists? One soft board is a repair. Widespread bounce usually traces to joists spaced too far apart for the boards, or to joist tops that have started to decay. Measure the joist spacing before choosing new boards. Composite needs closer spacing than many older wood decks were built with (see tab 3, "Upgrade from wood to Trex composite").

cards.title: Railings And Stairs That Move
cards.description: A rail that shifts when you lean on it is a safety problem, not a cosmetic one.

children.text: What Columbus requires A 36-inch guard wherever the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge A handrail 34–38 inches high on at least one side of any stair with 4 or more risers Stair risers no higher than 8¼ inches, treads at least 9 inches deep, and openings that won't pass a 4-inch sphere DCA 6 calls for guard posts of at least 4x4, bolted to joists or a rim of at least 2x8 and secured with hold-down hardware rated for 1,800 pounds. Railing posts depend on the frame. When the frame is replaced, the railing usually is too. Compare railing systems on
deck railings and accessories

cards.title: Rusted Hardware And Dark Stairs
cards.description: Corroded connectors and unlit steps are on NADRA's short list of deck warning signs.

children.text: Why the metal matters DCA 6 requires hot-dip galvanized or stainless steel fasteners and connectors with preservative-treated lumber. Rusted joist hangers, ledger bolts and post bases lose capacity long before they break. DCA 6 also calls for a light at the top landing that lights every stair, switched from inside the house. A replacement is the time to correct both.

cards.title: Can Trex Go On My Existing Frame?

children.text: joist spacing first Trex says joists for its decking should generally be no more than 16 inches on center. Diagonal boards need 12 inches, and heavier loads, longer spans or patterns can need 12 inches or less. Older wood decks were sometimes framed at 24 inches. Trex's fix is one new joist between each existing pair. Add-in joists can't make up for decay, a poor ledger or weak footings (see tab 1). Each board also needs its own fasteners and edge details for the line selected.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace my deck in Columbus?

children.text: For a rebuild, yes. Inside city limits, building a deck requires a permit and plan review. The only exception is a deck of no more than 200 square feet that is no more than 30 inches above grade, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Board-only resurfacing isn't listed separately in the city's documents, so its permit path is confirmed for your address. Outside the city, your local building department sets the rules.

items.question: Is resurfacing cheaper than a full replacement?

children.text: Usually, because the footings, posts and frame stay. But that only holds if the frame is sound. A resurfacing that has to add joists, replace a ledger and repair several joists can approach the cost of a rebuild. That's why we price both when the frame is borderline.

items.question: Will my new deck need new footings?

children.text: If the existing footings are too shallow, too small or were poured for posts in different places, yes. Footings must bear on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches deep or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Footings that meet the requirement and suit the new layout can stay, and the estimate says so.

items.question: Can you keep my existing railing or stairs?

children.text: Only if they're solid and fit the new deck. Railing posts and stair stringers attach to the frame, so a rebuilt frame usually means new ones. The new railing must meet Columbus's guard and handrail heights. Railing choices are covered on
deck railings and accessories

items.question: What happens to my old deck?

children.text: Taking it apart and hauling it away is part of the replacement. The estimate lists what comes off, how debris is removed and what is protected while we work.

items.question: Can the new deck be a different size?

children.text: Yes. A different size or shape changes the footings, framing, stairs and approvals, so it's planned as a new design. See
new deck installation
for layout questions.

items.question: Does a composite deck still need maintenance?

children.text: Less than wood, but some. Trex describes soap-and-water cleanup. Keep the board gaps clear of leaves so moisture doesn't sit on the frame, and check the drainage and the ledger area after storms. A wood deck needs its finish renewed; see
deck refinishing

items.title: What Gutter Guards Actually Do

children.text: Gutter guards sit over or within a gutter opening to reduce the amount of leaves and other material that enters the channel. They do not create extra drainage capacity or repair a sagging gutter. Water still has to pass through the guard, reach an outlet and move down the downspout.

A finer screen may limit more debris while requiring attention to material collecting on its surface. The right choice depends partly on the trees around your home and the shape of your roof.

Roof King & Restoration helps Columbus homeowners with ice dam removal and related roof damage. We inspect the affected roof areas, explain the removal work and identify repairs that may be needed after the ice clears.

opening.title: How to Recognize an Ice Dam

children.text: Icicles by themselves do not prove that a roof has an ice dam. Look for a solid ridge of ice at the eaves with snow or meltwater sitting above it. Water stains, damp insulation and active leaks near outside walls are warning signs of water entry.
Uneven snow melt can be another clue. If snow disappears from the upper roof while a thick frozen band remains at the edge, heat escaping into the attic may be warming the roof deck.
Signs worth reporting when you contact Roof King:
Ice forming in a continuous band along the roof edge or in a valley.
Ceiling stains, damp drywall or dripping near an exterior wall.
Water behind the fascia, or gutters pulling away under the weight of ice.
Repeated ice buildup on the same roof section after snowstorms.

opening.caption: The ice ridge blocks drainage at the eave. Blue arrows show meltwater and a possible route beneath the shingles into the roof or exterior wall.

items.tabLabel: Why Snow Melts and Refreezes at the Eaves
items.title: Why Snow Melts and Refreezes at the Eaves

children.text: Snow on a warmer part of the roof melts and flows downhill. When that water reaches the colder eave, it freezes again. Repeated melting and freezing can build a thick ridge of ice along the roof edge.

Warm air leaking into an attic, insulation gaps and some roof or ventilation conditions can warm the upper roof while the eaves remain below freezing. Weather and sun exposure can also affect the pattern.

items.tabLabel: How Water Backs Up Beneath the Shingles
items.title: How Water Backs Up Beneath the Shingles

children.text: As the ridge grows, it blocks normal runoff and creates a pocket of meltwater behind it. Water backed up against that barrier can reach gaps or vulnerable details beneath the roof covering. A roof does not have to sink or sag for this to happen.

Clogged gutters can add drainage problems, but clean gutters alone do not prevent ice dams. Ice can form on roofs without gutters, so gutter replacement or guards may leave the underlying cause untouched.

items.title: What to Do While Ice Is Building Up
items.tabLabel: What to Do While Ice Is Building Up

children.text: Keep people and pets away from heavy icicles or hanging ice. If water is entering the home, move belongings away from the leak where it is safe and document the visible damage. Avoid areas where water is near wiring or electrical fixtures and seek appropriate emergency assistance.

Do not climb onto a snowy or icy roof to chip at the buildup. Sharp tools can damage shingles and flashing. Avoid pressure washers, open flames and improvised heating methods; arrange a professional roof assessment instead.

When you contact Roof King, describe where the ice is forming, whether water has entered the house and whether the same spot has frozen before. Photos taken safely from the ground or indoors can help explain the problem.

items.question: Can ice dams cause roof leaks?

children.text: Yes. Meltwater can collect behind the frozen ridge and reach vulnerable areas beneath the roof covering. Water stains near outside walls, damp insulation and ceiling drips can indicate water entry.

items.question: Will cleaning my gutters stop ice dams?

children.text: Not by itself. Gutters need normal maintenance, but ice dams involve uneven roof temperatures and refreezing meltwater. They can form even where gutters are absent.

items.question: Is it safe to knock ice off the roof?

children.text: No. Climbing onto an icy roof and striking the ice can cause serious injury and damage the roof. Keep clear of unstable buildup and arrange a professional assessment.

items.question: How is ice dam removal planned for my roof?

children.text: Roof material, slope, ice thickness, access and active water backup determine the removal plan. The assessment identifies the affected area and precautions for the shingles, flashing and gutters, with any follow-up repairs addressed separately.

items.question: Does removing an ice dam fix a ceiling leak?

children.text: Removal may relieve the water backup, but damage to the roof, insulation or interior finishes still needs evaluation. A separate repair may be necessary after the ice clears.

items.question: Will insurance pay for ice dam damage?

children.text: Coverage depends on your policy, the cause of the damage and the insurer’s determination. Document the visible damage from a safe position and contact your insurer about the reporting process. Roof King’s assessment and estimate describe the roofing work; the insurer determines coverage.

items.question: Can gutter guards prevent ice dams?

children.text: Gutter guards can reduce certain debris problems. They do not control attic heat loss or guarantee that ice will not form at the roof edge.

opening.title: Common roof repairs in Dublin
opening.description: The right repair depends on which part of the roof has failed and what is happening around it. These are common areas we inspect when a roof leaks or shows visible damage.

items.title: Missing or damaged shingles

children.text: A limited area of missing, lifted or damaged shingles may be repairable when the surrounding roof is sound. The repair needs to account for the layers beneath the shingles and how the new material connects to the existing roof. Available products and weathering affect how closely the repair will match.

items.description: A limited area of missing, lifted or damaged shingles may be repairable when the surrounding roof is sound. items.label: Request a Repair Estimate

items.title: Pipe boots and roof vents

children.text: The flashing around a plumbing vent helps keep water out where the pipe passes through the roof. A split collar, damaged boot or poorly integrated flashing can leave an opening even when nearby shingles look fine. The inspection checks that connection and the surrounding roofing together.

items.description: The flashing around a plumbing vent helps keep water out where the pipe passes through the roof. items.title: Chimney and wall flashing

children.text: Where a roof meets a chimney, wall or dormer, flashing directs water across the transition. Loose pieces, damaged joints or poorly connected layers can let water behind the roof covering. A repair may involve exposing the connection and replacing the affected flashing and adjacent materials.

items.description: Where a roof meets a chimney, wall or dormer, flashing directs water across the transition. items.title: Valleys and roof edges

children.text: Valleys carry runoff from adjoining roof slopes. Roof edges connect the covering with the fascia and gutters. Damage, debris or an incomplete connection in these areas can change where water goes. Identifying the cause helps determine whether the work belongs in the roof, the drainage system or both.

items.question: Can a leaking roof be repaired without replacing it?

children.text: Often, yes, when the entry point is identifiable and the surrounding roof remains in serviceable condition. Widespread damage or deterioration can change that recommendation. An inspection establishes whether a focused repair will address the problem.

items.question: Can you assess a roof another company installed?

children.text: Contact Roof King with the property address and the issue you are seeing. Include any information about the existing roof and previous repairs. If a warranty may apply, check its terms before authorizing alterations.

items.question: Will the repaired shingles match the rest of the roof?

children.text: We look for a suitable match, but age, weathering and discontinued products can make an exact match difficult. Review the available material and any visible difference before agreeing to the repair.

items.question: How soon can the repair be completed?

children.text: Timing depends on current availability, safe access, weather, materials and the extent of the work. Tell us if water is entering now so the team can discuss the situation. A request through the website is not a confirmed appointment.

items.question: Is temporary protection the same as a completed repair?

children.text: No. Temporary protection is intended to limit further exposure while permanent work is arranged. If it is needed, confirm what it covers, how long it is intended to remain and which follow-up repairs are still required.

items.question: What warranty applies to a repair?

children.text: Coverage depends on the agreed work and the products used. Ask for the written terms for your repair, including the covered area, exclusions and contact for a concern. A manufacturer credential does not automatically give every repair an enhanced roof-system warranty.

items.question: Which roof areas are included?

children.text: Confirm the house, garage, additions and any separate structures you want addressed. Living area is not a substitute for roof measurement. Different shapes and slopes affect the surface area and work.

items.question: Which material and accessories are assumed?

children.text: A shingle category or metal option is not a complete specification. The final proposal needs the exact product and relevant underlayment, starter, ridge, flashing and other components for the selected system.

items.question: What removal and preparation are included?

children.text: The existing layers, disposal, access and supporting surface affect the project. An online result cannot establish every concealed condition. Ask which preparation items are assumed and which need inspection.

items.question: How are decking and other hidden repairs handled?

children.text: Covered damage may become visible only during work. The written estimate should explain how new findings are documented, priced and authorized. Do not treat an unexplained allowance as unlimited coverage for all repairs.

items.question: Which adjoining work is separate?

children.text: Gutters, siding, attic work and interior finishes can be related to a roofing project without being included in it. Identify those boundaries so the preliminary budget is not mistaken for a whole-property restoration price.

items.question: What is the biggest benefit of hiring a Master Elite contractor?

children.text: Access to Golden Pledge on a qualifying roof, together with a contractor who meets GAF’s certification and renewal requirements. It gives you a broader choice of manufacturer protection when you replace your roof.

items.question: Is Golden Pledge automatically included with every Roof King roof?

children.text: No. The roof must qualify, and the enhanced warranty must be selected and registered. Ask which warranty is included in your proposal.

items.question: How is GAF-backed workmanship protection different from a product warranty?

children.text: Product coverage concerns manufacturing defects. Misapplication coverage concerns covered installation errors. Golden Pledge includes both, with the covered products, flashings, remedies and conditions defined in its written terms.

items.question: Does lifetime coverage mean the roof never needs replacing?

children.text: No. Lifetime is a defined warranty term tied to eligible ownership and property types; it is not a prediction of roof life or a promise against all damage.

items.question: Can I choose my own shingle color and style?

items.title: Siding inspections after Columbus wind and hail storms

children.text: After a storm, loose panels, broken corners, dents or newly exposed wall areas deserve an inspection. We look at the visible damage and the connections around windows, doors and roof edges, where adjoining trim or flashing may also be affected.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace siding in Columbus?

children.text: Yes, inside city limits. Columbus lists replacement siding as requiring a building permit without plan review. State who applies in the agreement; other jurisdictions set their own requirements.

items.question: Can you replace siding on one side of the house?

children.text: Often. End new work at a corner, trim board or material change. A matching color name may still look different beside aged panels, so compare samples outside.

items.question: How long does siding replacement take?

children.text: Wall area, stories, layers to remove, hidden damage and weather all affect the sequence. Define the product and repairs before setting the expected schedule.

items.question: Will new siding lower energy bills?

children.text: That depends on the installed assembly. Insulated vinyl or a separate insulation layer changes the wall differently from a standard siding panel. Name the actual product and documented insulation value in the estimate.

items.question: Does insurance pay for storm-damaged siding?

children.text: Coverage depends on your policy and the insurer’s findings. Roof King documents the siding, trim and roof edge for the repair discussion.

items.question: What does the workmanship warranty cover?

children.text: Our 5-year workmanship warranty covers installation under the written project terms. Product defects are addressed by the manufacturer’s warranty; storm damage is considered separately.

items.question: Can I finance siding replacement?

children.text: Three- and five-year options are available, with payments as low as $47 on qualifying projects. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms. Compare the cash price, APR, fees and total repayment.

items.question: What is the best type of siding for a Columbus home?

children.text: Compare your priorities: vinyl for finished color and relatively low upkeep, LP SmartSide for engineered-wood profiles and finishes, and James Hardie for rigid fiber cement and architectural profiles. All need correct barrier and flashing details.

items.question: Is insulated vinyl the same as standard vinyl?

children.text: No. An insulated product has a backing with its own documented value. Name the product rather than assigning the same benefit to every vinyl panel or to fiber cement.

items.question: How does LP SmartSide handle moisture?

children.text: Its treatment and overlay work with sealed cut edges, clearances and a maintained finish. Keep sprinklers and gutter overflow from repeatedly wetting the siding.

items.question: Why does fiber cement cost more to install than vinyl?

children.text: Rigid boards need different handling, dust-controlled cutting and fastening. Primed boards also require paint. Compare complete installed prices rather than panel prices alone.

items.question: Can new siding match the existing panels?

children.text: Sometimes, but weathering and discontinued profiles can prevent a close match. Compare a sample outdoors and consider ending replacement at a natural break.

items.question: Can I paint siding later?

children.text: Primed engineered wood and fiber cement are intended for paint. Factory-finished products have their own care directions. Check the exact vinyl manufacturer’s painting guidance before coating vinyl.

items.question: Can different siding materials be used together?

children.text: Yes. Each material change needs suitable trim and flashing. Name the product and finish for every elevation and accent in the estimate.

cards.description: Damage you can see from the ground is enough to start with. Don't climb up or pull at loose material.

children.text: Stay out of rooms with sagging or soaked ceilings, and out of any building with visible structural damage until a professional clears it . If you smell gas, leave right away and call Columbia Gas from outside . Downed power lines are a 911 call . Don't use wet electrical equipment until a licensed electrician has checked it . Run a generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house .

cards.title: Slow the water down
cards.description: Temporary protection limits damage while the permanent repair is planned. It doesn't replace the repair.

children.text: Move belongings out of the way, catch drips and start drying wet materials within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold . If water is coming through the roof, call (614) 490-0123. Call Roof King to discuss temporary protection and inspection availability . Keep receipts for tarps, buckets, fans and any temporary repairs . Ask what the tarp covers and what permanent work is still needed.

cards.title: Photograph before you clean up
cards.description: Your own dated photos and video are the first part of the storm record.

children.text: Walk all four sides of the house and take wide shots from the ground, then close-ups of shingles in the yard, gutters, siding, screens and windows . Inside, photograph ceiling stains, wet insulation you can see from the attic hatch, and damaged belongings . Note the date and time of the storm and when you first noticed each problem. Don't throw out damaged items until your insurer says you can .

cards.title: Report the damage to your insurer yourself
cards.description: Policies can have reporting deadlines, so contact your insurer promptly and ask what records it needs .

children.text: Keep your policy number handy . Calling a roofer does not start a claim, and Roof King does not file one on your behalf . The
insurance claims tab
explains who does what.

cards.title: Find the storm date
cards.description: The storm report lists NOAA hail and wind reports near your address since 2019 .

children.text: These are reports, not a record of every hailstone. Hail falls in narrow bands, so a quiet result doesn't prove your roof is fine, and a nearby report doesn't prove it was hit . What the report gives you is a likely date.

items.title: What damage to look for

children.text: Storm damage rarely stops at the shingles. Here is what to look for on each part of the house, and which parts only show up when someone inspects the roof itself.

items.description: Storm damage rarely stops at the shingles. Here is what to look for on each part of the house, and which parts only show up when someone inspects the roof itself.

groups.title: What damage to look for — Details

cards.title: Shingles
cards.description: Missing, lifted or creased shingles after wind; bruising, cracks or exposed mat after hail .

children.text: Shingle pieces in the yard and fresh granules at the downspouts are clues. Granules also wash off as a roof ages, so they aren't proof on their own. Hail bruises rarely show from the ground, which is why Roof King photographs every slope, not just the side facing the street .

cards.title: Edges, flashing and vents
cards.description: Roof edges, ridges and the flashing at walls, chimneys and pipes are where wind gets a grip.

children.text: Look for bent or lifted metal at the roof edge, flashing pulled away from a wall or chimney, and dented or cracked vent caps. Roof King inspects flashing, penetrations, valleys and transitions one by one .

cards.title: Attic and ceilings
cards.description: New stains, damp insulation or daylight through the roof boards mean water or debris got through.

children.text: Look only from the attic hatch with a flashlight, and don't step between joists. Roof King checks the attic where there's access, for moisture and ventilation .

cards.title: Gutters and downspouts
cards.description: Dents, pulled hangers and sagging runs are common after hail and wind.

children.text: A dented gutter tells you hail fell. It doesn't, by itself, mean the shingles need replacing . Gutter, fascia and other soft-metal damage gets recorded separately during the inspection . See
gutter services

cards.title: Siding and trim
cards.description: Look for cracked, punctured or missing panels and dented trim, usually worst on the side that faced the storm.

children.text: Siding and trim damage should get its own lines on the estimate, separate from the roof. See
siding services

cards.title: Windows and screens
cards.description: Torn screens, cracked glass and dented frames or wraps.

children.text: Watch for new drafts or leaks around a window in the days after a storm. See
window replacement

items.title: Hail vs wind damage

children.text: The National Weather Service treats a thunderstorm as severe when it brings winds of 58 mph or more, hail 1 inch across or larger, or both . Smaller storms can still damage a worn roof, and a severe storm doesn't guarantee damage. Hail and wind also leave different patterns.
NWS Severe Thunderstorm Criteria

items.description: The National Weather Service treats a thunderstorm as severe when it brings winds of 58 mph or more, hail 1 inch across or larger, or both . Smaller storms can still damage a worn roof, and a severe storm doesn't guarantee damage. Hail and wind also leave different patterns.

cards.title: Hail damage
cards.description: Impact marks scattered across a slope: bruises, cracks, missing granules and dents in soft metal.

children.text: Damage can vary slope by slope, so the inspection marks and documents test squares on each slope where hail is suspected . Vents, gutters and flashing are recorded on their own, because a dent in metal doesn't prove the shingles are damaged . More on the
hail damage roof repair
page .

cards.title: Wind damage
cards.description: Wind damage starts at edges, ridges and corners and shows up as missing, lifted or creased shingles.

children.text: A shingle can lift, crease and lose its seal without blowing off, so the courses around a missing piece need checking too. Displaced flashing can open a gap at a wall or chimney . More on the
wind damage roof repair
page , and in
why fall gusts over 40 mph matter

cards.title: Trees and large debris
cards.description: A falling limb can break roof boards, rafters and gutters, not just shingles.

children.text: Have the tree removed by a tree professional before any roof work, and stay out of rooms below until the structure is checked . One customer's tree-damage job ended with new roofs and gutters on two homes .

items.question: Should I call my insurance company or a roofer first?

children.text: You can do both. Report the damage to your insurer promptly, because policies can have reporting deadlines . A Roof King inspection gives you written findings to share. Calling us does not start a claim .

items.question: What if I can't see any damage from the ground?

children.text: That's common with hail. Bruised shingles and lifted tabs rarely show from the yard. Tell us the storm date and any new leaks or stains, and stay off the roof. The inspection covers every slope .

items.question: Will Roof King deal with my insurance company for me?

children.text: No. In Ohio, negotiating or settling a property claim for a homeowner, for pay, is the work of a certified public insurance adjuster . Roof King provides the inspection photos, findings and estimate and explains them. You deal with your insurer .

items.question: Does storm damage mean I need a new roof?

children.text: Not necessarily. Isolated damage on a sound roof can often be repaired. Widespread damage, or shingles too worn to take a repair, points to replacement. The findings should show which applies.

items.question: Is the storm damage inspection free?

children.text: Yes. It's free with no obligation, and you keep the documented findings whether or not you hire Roof King .

items.question: Can you tarp my roof if it's leaking?

children.text: Call (614) 490-0123 and describe where the water is coming in. Ask about temporary protection and inspection availability . A tarp is temporary, and the estimate will list the permanent repair separately.

items.question: Do I need a permit for storm damage roof repair in Columbus?

children.text: Replacing a roof inside Columbus city limits requires a building permit, but not plan review, and historic districts may need extra approval . For a smaller repair, ask what your project needs. Get your storm damage inspected

items.title: Signs of hail damage

children.text: Real hail damage is random. Hits land scattered across a slope in different sizes, and the same storm marks the metal, siding and screens around the roof. A neat row of marks, or damage on one spot only, usually points to something else. Look from the ground or a window. Checking the roof surface is our job.

items.description: Real hail damage is random. Hits land scattered across a slope in different sizes, and the same storm marks the metal, siding and screens around the roof. A neat row of marks, or damage on one spot only, usually points to something else. Look from the ground or a window. Checking the roof surface is our job.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: Bruised shingles
cards.description: A hailstone can crush the asphalt and fiberglass mat under the granules without breaking the surface.

children.text: How a bruise shows up A dark, roughly round spot, often with granules pressed in or missing It gives slightly under a fingertip, like a soft spot on fruit. A blister doesn't. Bruises sit at random across the slope, more of them on the side that faced the storm They may not leak right away. The weakened spot can shed granules and crack later, which is why bruises are photographed and counted, not ignored.

cards.title: Granule loss
cards.description: Granules shield the asphalt from sun. Hail knocks them off in patches.

children.text: What granule loss does and doesn't prove Bare black spots on the shingle face, and heavy granules at downspout outlets after a storm Every roof sheds some granules with age, and new roofs shed loose ones in the first months. Granules in the gutter alone don't prove hail damage. What matters is exposed asphalt at impact points, matched to the storm date

cards.title: Cracks and mat fractures
cards.description: A hard hit can split the shingle and the fiberglass mat inside it.

children.text: Why fractures matter most A fracture is a break through the shingle. It can let water reach the underlayment. Fractures are hard to see from the ground and often show only when the shingle is lifted or flexed by hand The impact test behind Class 4 ratings fails a shingle when a crack shows on the back after two hits in the same spot, which is why fractures are treated as functional damage

cards.title: Soft metals on the roof
cards.description: Box vents, ridge vents, pipe flashing, valley metal, chimney caps and skylight curbs dent easily.

children.text: What dents tell us Dents show that hail hit and roughly how big it was, and which direction it came from A dented vent can be cosmetic, but a split or crushed one can leak Metal damage is recorded on its own line. A dented vent doesn't by itself mean the shingles failed.

cards.title: Gutters, downspouts and fascia
cards.description: Gutters often show the clearest hail marks on the house.

children.text: Cosmetic or functional Dents along the front lip and the top of downspout elbows A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often cosmetic. Split seams, crushed sections or pulled hangers aren't. Gutter work is quoted separately and handled through our
gutter services

cards.title: Siding, window screens and sills
cards.description: Hail strong enough to damage a roof usually marks the walls, fences and cars nearby too.

children.text: Check the side that faced the storm Cracked or holed vinyl siding, chipped paint on wood or fiber cement, dented aluminum trim Torn or dented window screens and dented metal window wraps Spatter marks on decks, fences and outdoor equipment help date the storm Siding repairs go through our
siding services
; windows through
windows

cards.title: Damage that only looks like hail
cards.description: Several roof problems get mistaken for hail.

children.text: Look-alikes we rule out Blisters: raised or popped bubbles from trapped moisture or heat. No bruise underneath. Normal wear: even granule thinning across a whole slope, often worst on the south and west faces Foot traffic or tools: scuffs near walkways, ladders and the ridge Old repairs or manufacturing marks: patterns that repeat across the roof. Hail doesn't make patterns.

items.title: Hail size and your roof

children.text: Size isn't everything. Shingle type, age, wind and the angle of impact all change what a storm does. Still, size is the first thing an adjuster and a roofer ask about, so it helps to know the reference points.

groups.title: Hail size and your roof — Details

cards.title: What forecasters call severe hail
cards.description: NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory considers hail quarter size, 1 inch across, or larger to be severe.

children.text: Size comparisons Quarter: 1 inch, the severe threshold Half dollar: roughly 1¼ inches Size means the diameter of the hailstone.

cards.title: When shingles start to show damage
cards.description: Damage depends on the shingle and its condition, not just the storm.

children.text: What one state regulator advises homeowners The Nebraska Department of Insurance says hail generally needs to be about 1¼ inches across before it damages a roof. Lightweight composite shingles can show damage from 1-inch hail, and only deteriorated shingles are usually damaged by hail under 1 inch. An older, brittle roof can be damaged by hail a newer roof shrugs off, which is why we look at the roof's age and condition alongside the storm.

cards.title: Wind-driven hail
cards.description: Hail falling at an angle hits one side of the house harder.

children.text: Why one slope can look worse Slopes, walls and screens facing the storm take more and harder hits. Slopes on the far side can be untouched. We record each slope separately for that reason.

cards.title: Finding the storm date
cards.description: Your insurer will ask when the damage happened.

children.text: Where storm reports come from NOAA's Storm Events Database records hail where someone reported it, such as a trained spotter, a law-enforcement officer or a member of the public. A report a mile away doesn't prove your roof was hit, and no nearby report doesn't prove it wasn't. Hail falls in narrow, uneven bands. Your own dated photos of hail on the ground, dented cars or spatter marks are often the best record.

items.title: Impact-resistant shingles (Class 4)

children.text: If hail means new shingles, it's worth looking at impact-rated lines. A UL 2218 Class 4 rating means samples survived a controlled test with a 2-inch steel ball. It's the highest class in that test. It doesn't make a roof hail-proof, and the rating describes new product in a lab.

cards.title: How UL 2218 works
cards.description: Steel balls are dropped onto shingles. Each class uses a bigger ball.

children.text: Class 1 to Class 4 Each class uses a larger steel ball. Class 4, the highest, uses a 2-inch ball dropped from 20 feet. The steel-ball size isn't a guaranteed safe hailstone size. Real hail varies in shape, density and speed. A shingle passes if no crack is visible on the back after two impacts in the same spot. FM 4473 uses the same class sizes Manufacturers reach Class 4 with a reinforcing scrim on the back or with polymer-modified (rubberized) asphalt that flexes on impact

cards.title: The limits of a lab rating
cards.description: A rating is a fair starting point for comparing lines, not a promise.

children.text: What the test doesn't cover Standard impact tests don't account for weathering, temperature or aging. Ridge caps and accessories may not carry the same rating as the field shingle. Ratings apply to labeled packages, so the bundle on your roof should match the line on the proposal.

cards.title: IBHS ratings with lab-made hailstones
cards.description: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety rates impact-resistant shingles with lab-made hailstones instead of steel balls.

children.text: How to use them IBHS grades shingles Excellent, Good, Marginal or Poor on dents, tears and granule loss. Its most recent ratings were released on November 19, 2025. Ask us to check where a line you're considering stands on the current list.

cards.title: What Ohio law says about claim negotiation
cards.description: In Ohio, negotiating a property claim settlement for pay is the job of a licensed public insurance adjuster.

children.text: Why your roofer shouldn't negotiate your settlement Ohio law defines a public insurance adjuster as anyone who, for compensation, acts for or helps an insured negotiate or settle a property claim, or advertises that service. No one may act as one without a certificate of authority from the state's superintendent of insurance. Roof King is a roofing contractor. We don't negotiate settlements or act as your adjuster. If you want someone to represent you, ask the Ohio Department of Insurance about licensed public adjusters. Be cautious of anyone who offers to "handle everything" with your insurer in exchange for signing a contract.
