items.question: What size hail damages a roof?

children.text: NOAA's severe-storm lab treats hail 1 inch across (quarter size) or larger as severe. Whether it damages your roof depends on the shingles and their age. The Nebraska Department of Insurance says damage generally starts around 1¼ inches, lightweight shingles can be damaged by 1-inch hail, and older, deteriorated shingles by smaller stones. An inspection settles it for your roof.

items.question: Can a roof have hail damage without leaking?

children.text: Yes. Bruises and small fractures often don't leak at first. They weaken the shingle so it loses granules and cracks over time. That's why we record and count hits after a storm instead of waiting for a stain on the ceiling. See the "Signs of hail damage" tab above.

items.question: Will Roof King handle my insurance claim?

children.text: No. You file the claim and talk with your insurer, and your insurer decides coverage and payment. We inspect the roof, document the damage and explain our findings and estimate so you can share them. We speak with your insurer only if you ask us to and we agree on it first. In Ohio, negotiating a claim settlement for pay is reserved for licensed public insurance adjusters. More on
storm damage documentation

items.question: Does a hail inspection cost anything?

children.text: No. Our inspection is no cost and no obligation, and you get written findings with photos whether or not you hire us. It typically takes 45 to 90 minutes, depending on the size and complexity of the roof.

items.question: Do Class 4 shingles lower my insurance premium?

children.text: Some insurers offer a credit for impact-rated roofs and some don't, so ask your insurer what it offers and what proof it needs. We can give you the product name and the documents from your project. Class 4 means a shingle passed the UL 2218 test with a 2-inch steel ball. It doesn't make a roof hail-proof. See the Class 4 lines in the tab above.

items.question: Does a dented gutter mean my roof needs replacing?

children.text: Not by itself. Gutters and vents dent more easily than shingles, so dents show that hail hit, not that the shingles failed. We check the shingles on their own and list gutters separately. A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often a cosmetic repair.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace a hail-damaged roof in Columbus?

children.text: Yes, inside city limits. The City of Columbus requires a building permit, without plan review, to replace a roof. Historic and special zoning districts such as German Village may need extra approvals, and suburbs set their own rules.

items.question: What if the roof is leaking now?

children.text: Call

, tell us where water is showing and when the storm hit, and ask about current availability. Until then, catch the water, move belongings and stay off the roof. Keep receipts for anything you do to protect the house. Temporary protection and the permanent repair are separate steps. See
storm damage repairs

groups.title: Deductibles, depreciation and what the insurer pays — Details

cards.title: Your deductible
cards.description: The deductible is the part of a covered loss you pay. Some policies set a separate wind, hail or roof deductible.

children.text: Be cautious with any offer to cover or waive your insurance deductible. The reason: the insurer pays from the price it's told. In Ohio, knowingly presenting a false or misleading statement to an insurer to defraud it is insurance fraud. If paying the deductible is the problem, see financing below.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Actual cash value (ACV)
cards.description: ACV pays the roof's replacement cost minus depreciation for age and wear.

children.text: Ohio's claims rule: the insurer determines actual cash value from the replacement cost at the time of loss, including sales tax, less depreciation, and must give you documentation of the depreciation on request. NAIC's illustration: $15,000 of roof damage with $10,000 of depreciation and a $1,000 deductible pays $4,000 under ACV, against $14,000 under replacement cost. figures, not a Roof King price.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Replacement cost value (RCV)
cards.description: RCV pays to repair or replace the roof without subtracting depreciation, less your deductible.

children.text: Insurers often pay the actual cash value first and reimburse the withheld amount, called recoverable depreciation, after the work is done and the invoice is submitted. items.question: Can Roof King file or negotiate my insurance claim?

children.text: No. You file the claim and deal with your insurer. Ohio requires a public adjuster license to negotiate or settle a claim for compensation, and ODI advises homeowners not to let a contractor do it. We inspect, document the damage and explain the process so you can make your own decisions.

items.question: Should I call my insurer or a roofer first?

children.text: Contact your insurer promptly; Columbus warns that claims often have reporting deadlines. An inspection helps you see whether the damage likely exceeds your deductible. Whether to file a claim is your decision, and we'll give you clear information to make it.

items.question: Will you cover or waive my deductible?

children.text: Be cautious with any contractor who offers to. The deductible is your share of a covered loss, and misleading an insurer about the price is insurance fraud in Ohio. Financing can spread the cost: 3- or 5-year options on qualifying projects, subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

items.question: What's the difference between ACV and replacement cost on a roof claim?

children.text: Actual cash value is the replacement cost minus depreciation; Ohio's rule lets you ask for documentation of every depreciation deduction. Replacement cost pays without subtracting depreciation, less your deductible, though insurers often hold part back until the work is finished.

items.question: How long does an Ohio insurer have to respond to my claim?

children.text: Under Ohio's claims rule, 15 days to acknowledge it, and 21 days from a properly executed proof of loss to accept or deny it. If it needs longer, it must tell you why and update you in writing at least every 45 days.

items.question: What if the insurer's estimate is lower than yours?

children.text: Compare them line by line. If items are missing, send the insurer our photos and estimate and ask, in writing, for a re-inspection or revised estimate. We explain our findings; the amount is settled between you and your insurer.

items.question: My claim was denied. What now?

children.text: Read the policy provision the denial cites; Ohio requires the insurer to name it. Ask ODI's consumer services team through its official website about your options, or consider a licensed public adjuster or attorney. You can still repair the damage, with financing if needed.

items.question: Can I trust a contractor who knocks on my door after a storm?

children.text: Check before you sign. ODI recommends verifying registration with the Ohio Secretary of State, getting more than one estimate and watching any inspection. Columbus residents can also look up licensed contractors on the City's Citizen Access Portal.

On August 11, 2026, the National Weather Service measured an 82 mph gust at John Glenn Columbus International Airport and 70 mph at the Ohio State University Airport, and it attributed widespread Franklin County damage to straight-line winds of 60–80 mph . After a storm like that, the order matters: stay safe, limit water getting in, record the damage, then have the roof inspected.
NWS Franklin County Storm Survey — August 11, 2026

cards.title: Stay safe and stay off the roof
cards.description: Wind-damaged roofs are slick, loose and sometimes carrying limbs or wires.

children.text: Before anything else Contact emergency services for downed power lines, a structural collapse or fire. If you smell gas, leave the house and contact your gas utility from outside. Stay out of rooms or buildings with visible structural damage until a professional has checked them. Look and photograph from the ground or from inside. Don't climb up or pull at loose shingles, flashing or limbs.

cards.title: Slow the water down
cards.description: Temporary protection buys time. It isn't the repair.

children.text: What temporary protection does and doesn't do Inside: move belongings, catch drips and start drying wet materials. The City of Columbus advises starting within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold. On the roof: a temporary cover over an opening is installed where it's appropriate and available. Call (614) 490-0123 and describe the problem so availability can be discussed. Keep receipts for emergency supplies, temporary repairs and professional services. Temporary protection doesn't seal broken shingle bonds or reattach flashing. The estimate should say what it covers and what permanent work remains.

cards.title: Record it before cleanup
cards.description: Photos taken the day of the storm are the best record you'll have.

children.text: What to record Photos and video of every damaged area inside and out, with the date and time Shingles, ridge pieces, flashing or gutter sections in the yard. Photograph them where they landed and keep them. Ceiling stains, drips and attic wetness Don't throw away damaged items until your insurance carrier says it's acceptable. Our
storm documentation page
explains how inspection photos, the estimate and completed-work records fit together.

items.title: Shingles and seal strips

children.text: Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.

items.description: Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: Broken seal strips
cards.description: A shingle can look flat and still be unsealed.

children.text: Why the bond matters IBHS notes that wind can lift unsealed shingles and let water seep underneath. New shingles can take one to two months or more to seal in poor conditions. We check courses by hand on the windward slopes, where wind usually breaks the most bonds. A shingle that lifts freely along a whole course points to a wider bond failure, not a single loose piece.

cards.title: Creased shingles
cards.description: When wind lifts a shingle and drops it, the mat can fold across the nail line.

children.text: Why a crease counts as damage A crease is a break in the shingle's mat. It won't lie flat again or reseal reliably. Creases usually run in a line across several shingles on the same course. Creased shingles are replaced. Gluing them down leaves the fold in place.

cards.title: Missing shingles and exposed nails
cards.description: A blown-off shingle leaves nail heads and the course above it exposed.

children.text: What sits under the gap Exposed nails and nail holes let water track down into the underlayment and deck. We check whether the shingles around the gap were nailed correctly, because nail position affects how a shingle holds in wind. Underlayment and decking under the opening are checked before new shingles go on.

cards.title: Granules and scuffs
cards.description: Bare spots and fresh scuffs show where shingles flapped or debris dragged.

children.text: How we read them A heavy pile of granules at the downspouts after a storm is worth mentioning when you call. Scuffs alone may be cosmetic. Scuffs with lifted or creased shingles usually aren't. Hail leaves a different pattern. See
hail damage roof repair
if the storm brought both.

items.title: Ridges, edges, flashing and gutters

children.text: Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

items.description: Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

groups.title: Ridges, edges, flashing and gutters — Details

cards.title: Ridge and hip caps
cards.description: Ridge caps sit on the most exposed line of the roof.

children.text: What fails and how it's fixed Caps crack or blow off, exposing the ridge vent or the shingle tops underneath. Hip and ridge caps are made to bend over the seam and are fastened on each side above the sealant strip. A lost run of caps is replaced with a compatible cap product, and the ridge vent is checked for wind damage.

cards.title: Eaves and rakes
cards.description: Wind gets under the first course at the eaves and along the gable rakes.

children.text: Why the edge needs attention IBHS says the starter strip helps prevent water intrusion and protects against wind uplift at the roof edges. We check the starter course, the drip edge and the first shingle course for lifting. An edge that was never properly started tends to fail again. The estimate should say how the new edge will be built.

cards.title: Flashing
cards.description: Wind loosens step flashing, counterflashing and chimney flashing, opening a path for water.

children.text: What we check Step flashing along walls and dormers, chimney flashing and counterflashing, skylight and vent flanges Bent, lifted or face-caulked pieces are reset or replaced, not coated over The repair names the failed part rather than treating everything as a shingle replacement

cards.title: Gutters and downspouts
cards.description: Wind and falling limbs pull gutters away from the fascia and bend downspouts.

children.text: Gutters belong in the same inspection Gutters pulled from the fascia can let water behind them onto the fascia board and the roof edge. We note gutter and fascia damage separately on the estimate, not folded into the roof patch. Gutter repair and replacement are covered on our
gutter services page

items.title: Fallen trees and limbs

children.text: A tree or a large limb on the roof is a structural problem first and a roofing problem second. The roof can only be repaired properly once the tree is off and the framing and decking below have been checked.

cards.title: Before the tree comes off

children.text: Safety first If lines are down or the structure is damaged, contact emergency services and stay clear. Photograph the tree on the roof from the ground and the damage from inside before anything is moved. A tree blocking the street can be reported to the City of Columbus. Damage entirely on private property is the owner's and their insurer's responsibility.

children.text: What the inspection covers Broken or cracked decking and any damaged rafters or trusses under the impact area Shingles, ridge, flashing and gutters along the path the tree took Siding, fascia and soffit damage where the tree hit the wall line Damaged wood is noted for repair before new roofing goes on

items.title: Wind ratings and shingles

children.text: Shingle packages list wind classifications from two different ASTM tests, plus a separate manufacturer wind warranty. They answer three different questions, and none of them means a roof can't be damaged by wind.

items.description: Shingle packages list wind classifications from two different ASTM tests, plus a separate manufacturer wind warranty. They answer three different questions, and none of them means a roof can't be damaged by wind.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: ASTM D3161 (Class A, D, F)
cards.description: A fan-driven test of shingles on a test deck.

children.text: What the class means IBHS describes D3161 as measuring a shingle's ability to withstand fan-induced wind speeds. Class F is the highest D3161 class. GAF lists it as 110 mph. The speed describes air flowing over the shingles in the lab, not the wind load on your house.

cards.title: ASTM D7158 (Class D, G, H)
cards.description: An uplift test that measures how strongly the sealed shingle resists being pulled up.

children.text: What the class means IBHS: D7158 assigns a class based on a two-part uplift test, and the classes tie to ASCE 7 wind zones. Class H is the highest D7158 class. GAF lists it as 150 mph. Both tests evaluate new product. IBHS notes they don't account for weathering or aging. An older roof doesn't keep its rating.

cards.title: Wind warranty is a separate promise
cards.description: A limited wind warranty is the manufacturer's coverage terms, not a test result.

children.text: What usually decides coverage The stated mph applies to a particular product, installed a particular way. Higher wind coverage often requires the manufacturer's starter, ridge and other accessories, extra nails or a special application. The product cards below show each line's conditions. Shingles generally need to have sealed. Damage from falling trees or debris is a different matter from blow-off. Your proposal names the product, and the manufacturer's warranty document sets the terms.

How that applies to your roof is the insurer's decision under your policy. We document the product on your roof and what's currently available.

children.text: Most wind damage is repairable. Wind alone doesn't make a roof a replacement case, and you should expect a clear reason before anyone recommends one.

cards.title: When a repair makes sense
cards.description: Damage is limited to identifiable areas and the surrounding shingles still bond and flex.

cards.title: When replacement belongs in the conversation
cards.description: Bond failure is widespread, or the shingles are too brittle to work.

children.text: Signs a repair won't last Seal strips broken across whole slopes, not just a few courses Old shingles crack when lifted to weave in new ones Repeated blow-offs, or decking damage across a large area Our

items.question: How strong does wind have to be to damage a roof?

children.text: There's no single number. Shingle age, how well the courses sealed, nailing, roof shape and exposure all matter. Wind ratings are measured on new shingles in a lab, and IBHS notes the tests don't account for weathering or aging. Older roofs, edges and ridges usually fail first. After any storm that sends shingles into the yard, have the roof checked.

items.question: Can a few blown-off shingles be repaired, or does the whole roof need replacing?

children.text: Most wind damage is repairable. A repair makes sense when the damage is confined to identifiable areas and the surrounding shingles still seal and bend without cracking. Replacement belongs in the conversation when seal strips have failed across whole slopes or the old shingles are too brittle to work. You'll get the reason in writing either way. See
roof repair
for repairs beyond storm damage.

items.question: Will new shingles match the rest of my roof?

children.text: Often closely, but rarely perfectly. Weathering, color batches and discontinued lines all affect the match. We identify your shingle, show you the closest current product and tell you how it will look before work starts. For insured losses on a replacement-cost policy, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace enough for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's call.

items.question: Does homeowners insurance cover wind damage to a roof?

children.text: That depends on your policy and is decided by your insurer, not by Roof King. Contact your carrier promptly, because policies have reporting deadlines. We can inspect, photograph and document the damage and give you a written estimate for the work. The
storm documentation page
explains what those records contain.

items.question: Will Roof King negotiate my claim or act as my adjuster?

children.text: No. In Ohio, acting for a homeowner in settling a property claim for compensation is public insurance adjusting, which requires a state certificate of authority. We explain our construction findings and the proposed work. You may share our written construction findings with your insurer; coverage and payment remain between you and the insurer.

items.question: A tree fell on my roof. What should I do first?

children.text: Get everyone clear. Contact emergency services if power lines are down or the structure looks unsafe, and stay out of damaged rooms. Photograph the tree and the damage from the ground and from inside before anything is moved, and contact your insurer. Once the tree is off, the roof inspection should check the decking and framing under the impact, not just the shingles.

items.question: Do I need a permit for wind damage roof work in Columbus?

children.text: Inside City of Columbus limits, replacing a roof requires a building permit, with no plan review. Properties in special zoning or historic districts may need extra approvals. Ask whether your repair needs a permit and who will pull it. Suburbs outside the city set their own rules.

items.question: What do wind ratings and wind warranties on new shingles mean?

children.text: ASTM D3161 (up to Class F) and ASTM D7158 (up to Class H) are two different lab tests of new shingles. A limited wind warranty is the manufacturer's coverage, and higher speeds often depend on qualifying accessories and installation. For example, GAF's WindProven coverage requires a qualifying system. Neither makes a roof wind-proof. The Wind ratings tab above compares four lines we show on our site.

opening.title: What to Do First When a Storm Damages Your Roof

items.tabLabel: Stay off the roof and avoid hazards
items.title: Stay off the roof and avoid hazards

children.text: Wet shingles and storm debris make roof access dangerous. If a tree has struck the house, a ceiling is sagging or water is near wiring, keep people away from the affected area. Contact emergency services or the utility company when conditions require it. Do not climb onto the roof to take photographs.

items.label: Request a Storm Damage Inspection

items.tabLabel: Photograph the damage from a safe location
items.title: Photograph the damage from a safe location

children.text: Take pictures of the house from the ground, including the roof edges, gutters, siding and fallen debris. Photograph interior stains or active leaks as well. Record the storm date and save the original photos. These details help explain what changed and where an inspector should look.

items.label: Request a Storm Damage Inspection

items.tabLabel: Protect the interior without creating another hazard
items.title: Protect the interior without creating another hazard

children.text: Move belongings away from active leaks when it is safe to do so. If temporary protection is needed, ask a qualified contractor what can be done safely. Keep receipts and photographs of any temporary work. Temporary protection is not a permanent roof repair.

items.label: Request a Storm Damage Inspection

items.tabLabel: Arrange an inspection before deciding on replacement
items.title: Arrange an inspection before deciding on replacement

children.text: One missing shingle does not automatically mean the entire roof needs to be replaced. The right recommendation depends on the extent of the damage, the roof's age and condition, and whether water reached the materials underneath.

items.question: Can wind damage a roof without blowing shingles off?

children.text: Yes. Wind can lift shingles and weaken their sealant bonds without leaving a visible gap from the ground. An inspection can help determine whether the affected shingles remain serviceable.

items.question: Do hail dents on gutters mean my roof needs replacement?

children.text: No. Dents are evidence that hail struck a surface, but the roof covering needs its own assessment. Metal marks alone do not establish that every shingle has functional damage.

items.question: How soon should I schedule a roof inspection after a storm?

children.text: Arrange an inspection reasonably promptly if you see missing shingles, loose flashing, fallen debris or interior water staining. If there is an immediate safety hazard, address that first.

items.question: Will homeowners insurance pay for storm damage roof repairs?

children.text: It may, depending on your policy and the cause and extent of the damage. The insurance company determines coverage. Roof King can document roofing conditions and provide a repair or replacement estimate.

items.question: Can Roof King repair storm-damaged siding and gutters too?

children.text: Roof King offers roofing, siding and gutter services. The assessment can identify related exterior damage so the appropriate work is described and priced separately.

items.question: Does a small roof leak mean I need a new roof?

children.text: Not necessarily. A localized flashing or shingle problem may be repairable. Repeated leaks, widespread storm damage or deteriorated roofing materials can change the recommendation.

items.question: Is a free inspection the same as an insurance adjustment?

children.text: No. A roofing inspection addresses the condition of the roof and possible construction work. Your insurer evaluates coverage under the policy.
